v1.feedback: The leaf-as-unit golden-angle spiral reads clearly and the halcyon palette shift (cerulean, sage, pale gold) is well-chosen — restrained and coherent. However the 'halcyon' morph mostly just recolored the parent and slowed the rotation; the water plane beneath is a nice touch but too faint to register as a real compositional element. Push the morph further: let leaves actually settle onto the water surface over time (vertical collapse animation), add subtle per-leaf transparency fade at the spiral edges to evoke dissipation, and increase the water plane's opacity/wave amplitude so it becomes a legible ground plane rather than a ghost layer.

v2.feedback: The golden-angle phyllotaxis spiral settling onto water is a legible read on the parent's leaf-as-unit concept, and the halcyon word clearly drove the cerulean/sage/gold palette and the gentle descent animation — good chain lineage. Two issues: the 144 leaves are MeshPhong meshes, not particles, so this is closer to a scene than a particle piece, and the settle animation finishes after ~26s leaving a static flat raft with only slow rotation and breathing — add a second-act behavior (leaves lifting in thermals, re-spiraling, or dissolving into particle trails) so the piece doesn't die. The water plane's edge fade uses gl_FragCoord.xyz distance which is screen-space nonsense for fog — use view-space depth instead, and tighten the plane radius so the transparent edges don't bleed awkwardly at wide aspect ratios.
